message.subject: Re: Single source review: alias directory observation candidate
message.body:
Source review of alias_observation.go and its single ts.go call in the enola-watch-fanout worktree. Read-only, no edits, no builds, no tests, no measurement. Reviewed against the uncommitted tree at 9bf667d plus overlay.go, observe.go, discoverywalk.go, discovery.go, session.go, vue.go and inputscope/scope.go.

VERDICT. I found no defect that changes output on a quiescent tree, and the design sidesteps the trap I would have expected first. The reuse is conservative in the right direction: on a miss it falls through to the real reader, and the probe ledger it consumes is written under the same policy scope. Three things are worth your attention before acceptance, one of which I would fix now because it is cheap, and the remaining ones are a semantic statement to record rather than code to change. Details and the exact reasoning below, including what I checked and could not fault.

WHAT MAKES IT SAFE, verified rather than assumed.

1. The observation ledger is unchanged, which is the property that matters most. On a reuse hit nothing is recorded, and recordDir is first-wins, so the alias walk's own overlayReadDir call was already contributing nothing for those directories before the change. On a miss the call falls through to overlayReadDir, which records exactly as before. inputscope ReadDir has no side effects beyond the read itself: no counters, no error ledger, no violation recording. So seen, stat and dirs are byte-for-byte what they were, which is what your test asserts on all three snapshots and what the retained-discovery reobservation fence consumes. That is the strongest single argument for the change and it holds.

2. The testdata trap is avoided by construction, not by luck. discoveryPruned prunes hidden directories, tsSkipDirs and testdata, while the alias walk prunes only hidden and tsSkipDirs, so the two walks disagree about testdata. Reuse is keyed on completed enumerations rather than on the pruned entry list: overlayWalkDir deletes a SkipDir'd directory from enumerated, so testdata itself is never in probe.dirs and the alias walk's descent into it falls through to a live read. Crucially the testdata name is still present in the parent's recorded set, because set[d.Name()] is written before fn is called, so the parent listing is not missing the entry. I checked this specifically because a prior sharing attempt in this area lost testdata; this one does not.

3. Recorded sets and live listings are the same set under the same policy. Scope.ReadDir filters children with Allowed(join(dir, name), d.IsDir()); Scope.WalkDir's wrapper applies Allowed(path, d.IsDir()) at visit time and returns SkipDir for a refused directory, so the callback never sees it and it is never recorded. Same predicate, same arguments. An excluded directory is never recorded at all, so it always falls through to overlayReadDir and still gets its fs.ErrNotExist. Entry kinds match too: both paths derive from ReadDir-sourced DirEntries through entryKind, and aliasObservedEntry reports IsDir false for a symlink exactly as a real DirEntry does, which is why your linked fixture produces identical roots.

4. Ordering is preserved. os.ReadDir returns entries sorted by name and WalkDir visits in that order; the reuse path sorts by Name, names are unique within a directory so the comparator is a total order, and aliasRoots therefore accumulate in the same order as before. That matters because downstream alias resolution is order-sensitive.

5. Only Name and IsDir are consulted on the namesOnly path: the recursion at ts.go 3294-3297, and aliasesAtDirFromListing, which uses Name only and passes paths, not entries, to tryParseTSConfigAliases. Nothing calls Info, which would get fs.ErrInvalid. The visit path keeps real entries.

6. Locking is correct: the mutex is taken, the map is copied into fresh values, the mutex is released unconditionally before the sort and before any fall-through, so no lock is held across overlayReadDir and there is no double-unlock path. The recorded name maps are read, never retained or mutated, which matches dirSnapshot's ownership comment.

7. The scope of engagement is narrower than the guard suggests, and today that is correct. withOverlayProbe has exactly one non-test call site, discovery.go 83, which installs the probe and the walk cache together with e.inputScope, one Policy for the whole build. CompositionSignature at session.go 1385 installs a walk cache with no probe, so probeFrom returns nil and the config-inventory path at session.go 1295 keeps live reads, as does ts.go 242 and ts.go 4813. So the single-call, discovery-only claim is accurate as written.

RISK 1, the one I would act on. The guard does not check Allowed(dir, true), and it does not key on policy identity. probe.dirs is keyed by absolute path only, so the safety of serving a recorded listing to a caller rests on there being exactly one Policy per probe. That invariant holds today because the only probe is created next to e.inputScope, but nothing in aliasDirectoryEntries enforces it, and the vue.go precedents that read the same map do check scope.Allowed before trusting it. Two cheap hardenings that cost nothing on the hit path: add scope.Allowed(dir, true) to the guard for parity with vue.go, and state the one-policy-per-probe invariant in the comment so a future second probe site does not silently inherit a listing filtered under a different policy. Note also that today the effective gate is probe AND cache AND policy, and the discovery-only restriction is enforced by the absence of a probe on CompositionSignature's context rather than by anything in this function; if a probe is ever attached there, reuse starts applying to composition signatures without any change here.

RISK 2, the semantic shift to record. This is the answer to your first-listing question. Before the change the alias walk read the tree at alias-walk time; after it, for every directory the earlier collectors fully enumerated, alias roots are a function of the enumeration taken at that earlier moment. In newDiscovery that window is the interval between the shared walk around line 98 and collectTSAliasRoots at line 113. Within it, a directory created on disk is now invisible to the alias walk where a live read would have seen it, so a new package's tsconfig can be missed for that build. This is not a fence weakness and not a cross-run change: aliasRoots was already a retained-discovery output reused wholesale under the same reobservation fence, so cross-run behaviour is untouched. It is also not reachable from the capture alone, because a captured path whose parent directory is not on disk was invisible to a live ReadDir as well, and aliasesAtDirFromListing already compensates for a captured config at an enumerated directory, which your third test pins. So the exposure is exactly genuine within-run mutation. My position, consistent with what I have said before, is that the short window is not itself a proof of safety; what makes this acceptable is that it reduces rather than increases the number of independent observations, so discovery and the alias set are now pinned to one time basis instead of two that could already disagree. That is a defensible property, and it deserves one sentence in the comment saying so, because the sentence presently there argues cross-run fence coverage, which is true but is not what protects this change.

RISK 3, error-path divergence, narrow but real. The reuse path always returns a nil error, so a directory that was enumerated earlier and became unreadable since no longer produces listingErr, no longer takes the aliasesAtDir fallback, and no longer stops the recursion; children are visited from the stale names and each then hits its own record or a fresh failing read. The direction is benign, since the fallback existed to salvage unreadable directories and reuse has a listing to work from instead, and alias discovery is if anything more robust. But the traversal shape under concurrent deletion differs from the baseline, so it belongs in the same recorded semantic statement as risk 2 rather than being left implicit.

TWO SMALLER POINTS. The local named complete is the map-presence boolean, not a computed completeness check; it reads correctly only because recordDir's contract stores nothing but completed enumerations, so a reader may look for a validation that is not there. One word of comment fixes it. And aliasObservedEntry.Type collapses every non-directory, non-symlink kind to a regular file, so a socket, fifo or device entry would report Type 0 rather than its real bits; nothing on this path consults Type today, and the comment already says this is not a general filesystem entry, so this is a note for whoever adds the next consumer rather than a defect.

TEST COVERAGE, where I would add cases. What is covered is good: symlink, testdata, policy exclusion, a case-folded config name, ledger equality on all three snapshots, cross-run membership refusal, and a captured config absent from the listing. Three gaps, all about the behaviour the change actually alters. First, there is no test in which the recorded listing is stale relative to the live tree; the equivalence test compares the two paths on a quiescent tree, which by construction cannot observe the one difference that exists, so the intended behaviour under within-run creation is unpinned. A test that runs sharedDiscoveryEntries, then creates a directory with a tsconfig, then asserts the chosen semantics would make risk 2 a decision rather than an accident. Second, nothing covers a directory that was enumerated and then became unreadable, which is risk 3. Third, nothing covers the enumerated-and-empty recorded set, which overlayWalkDir deliberately stores as a real observation and which reuse now serves as an empty listing. I am not asking for these before acceptance; I am saying which properties are currently asserted by argument rather than by test.

ON THE MICRODIAGNOSTIC. Your labelling is right and I would keep it. Six in-process pairs with counterbalanced order, one process, one warm tree, timings taken with time.Now around two code paths inside a test, are a mechanism diagnostic, not an acceptance sample, and the 67 ms against 14 ms figure is a comparison of a warm-dentry live re-read against a map copy, so it is an upper bound on what the alias walk can stop paying inside a build where the shared walk already read those directories, not an end-to-end saving. The shared walk still happens and its cost is outside both timed regions. Both arms are symmetric on cache warmth because the candidate arm performs no filesystem reads at all, so the counterbalancing is not compromised; the limit is isolation and process freshness, not order. Any performance claim should wait for a fresh-process CLI cohort under the usual frozen rule, and nothing here supports a general speedup statement.

ONE HYGIENE NOTE. TestDiagnosticAliasObservedProduct lives in the production package's test file, is env-gated and skips by default, but it pulls gopkg.in/yaml.v3 into the package's test dependencies and embeds a shared-host Product diagnostic in the unit suite. That is the same separation you asked me to keep for my own diagnostics, where the file stays scratch and is reported as such. Your call; it does not affect correctness.

WHAT I DID NOT DO. No edits, no reruns, no builds, no tests, no timing, and nothing in the worktree touched; I read only. I did not attempt to reproduce the 22.571 s suite result or the micro pairs, and I am not asserting anything about them beyond what the source shows. Remaining source-only and retained.
